DJemma: Hands-Free Music-Making with On-Device Gemma

Community Article Published
November 23, 2026 Upvote 10 Dima Dobrynin ddbrx litert-community SF Yoursmiling litert-community

The problem

Mobile interfaces assume touch or voice input, but many people can't use either, e.g. individuals with cerebral palsy.
Some phones have head control, but it usually emulates a finger: one gesture per tap. That works for menus, not for anything expressive.
We built a third way in: head control that understands intent, powered by Gemma 4. It runs fully on the phone: private, offline, no network lag. Music is our test case because it's the least forgiving: real-time and expressive.

What we built

DJemma is an app where you play the melody with your face, and Gemma acts as your DJ.

You play. Turn your head to pick a note and open your mouth to play it. Notes snap to the scale and the beat, so there are no wrong notes. Widen or narrow your eyes to change the tempo.

You set the direction. Pick an instrument, a mood or a photo, and Gemma 4's vision turns the picture into a matching mix:

Or head-type your own request, like "rain on a window", with Gemma predicting the next word so each pick goes further:

DJemma follows you. Every few bars, Gemma reads how you've been playing and adjusts the backing: drums in when you pick up, space when you go quiet. Each change shows up on screen in plain words. You lead; the AI supports your choices.

Full Demo: YouTube.
Code: github.com/ddbrx/gemma4-hack-djemma

How we used LiteRT

Both models run on Google's on-device stack: MediaPipe for face tracking, and Gemma 4 E2B through LiteRT-LM for everything else. The app doesn't request the internet permission, and we demoed in airplane mode.
Hardware. We demoed on a Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, a mid-range phone, to show this works on a phone people actually own, not only on a flagship.
Face tracking. MediaPipe Face Landmarker in live-stream mode at about 640×480, one face. The head-pose matrix drives the pointer, and blendshapes detect mouth and eye gestures. It tries the GPU delegate first and falls back to the CPU.
Gemma 4 E2B via LiteRT-LM. One model does three jobs: it DJs, it reads mood photos with vision, and it predicts words for head-typing. E2B is small enough to share the phone with the camera, tracking and audio. To keep it fast, we prefilled each system prompt ahead of time, so a request only has to process its own few lines. For the DJ, Gemma replies with a short list of commands from a fixed vocabulary (intensity, layers, tempo, key, preset). The app validates and clamps every command and drops anything malformed, so the model can't break the music.

What we learned

Keep the model out of the timing loop. Music needs millisecond timing, and Gemma takes about a second per decision. Splitting the app into a fast loop (camera to sound) and a slow loop (Gemma to backing track) made both work. If your device has to perceive, reason and act, decide early which loop each part lives in.
Show the AI's work. Our first UI had separate Play and Band screens, so nobody saw Gemma react to their playing. Merging them into one screen, with DJemma's changes written out in plain words, made the concept click instantly. Naming the AI after the product helped too: nobody asked what Gemma does.
A fixed vocabulary beats free text. A small model reliably picks from a short list of well-described commands. Capping it at two changes per decision kept it from overreacting.
Don't block on predictions. Typing with your head is slow, and waiting a second after every letter for a prediction makes it feel even slower. Run predictions in the background, keep the old suggestions on screen until new ones arrive, and fall back to a simple offline predictor when Gemma isn't ready. A one-gesture undo matters more than prediction accuracy.

What's next

We plan to bring this kind of AI-assisted control into the spatial interaction interfaces we're building at Staxel AI, where we turn displays into touchless surfaces using a standard webcam and on-device AI. We've already started: since the hackathon, we've added head tracking to Staxel TouchlessOS as an accessibility mode on our public displays.

Next, we're upgrading Staxel Board, our touchless letterboard app for non-verbal people who can't use traditional touch devices. Today it uses hand tracking only, with basic next-word prediction, and runs only on iOS. We're adding head tracking, Gemma 4-powered word and intent prediction, and an Android version.

We also plan to bring Gemma 4 across our apps: adapting movement-based learning games to each child's pace, and helping public displays understand what a visitor is trying to do, not just where they're pointing. The same idea as DJemma: let the user lead, and let on-device AI make every action count.
